lesson.title: The Repeating Pattern Inside a Crystal
lesson.summary: Crystalline solids are built from a highly ordered, repeating arrangement of particles called a crystal lattice, which gives them sharp melting points and often distinctive geometric shapes, as seen in quartz and table salt.
lesson.body:
A crystalline solid is a solid in which the particles, atoms, ions, or molecules, are arranged in a highly ordered, repeating three-dimensional pattern that extends throughout the entire sample. This ordered pattern is the crystal lattice you have already encountered: a repeating arrangement built from a smallest repeating unit, the unit cell, which stacks in all three directions to build up the full structure. Because the same small unit repeats with essentially perfect regularity, the internal order of a crystalline solid is often described as long-range order, meaning the pattern you see around any one particle predicts the pattern around a particle far away in the same crystal.

This long-range order is what produces the flat faces and characteristic geometric shapes visible in many natural crystals. Quartz, a crystalline form of silicon dioxide (SiO2), grows into the recognizable six-sided prisms often seen in mineral samples precisely because its internal silicon and oxygen atoms are locked into a repeating tetrahedral lattice, and the external facets reflect the internal symmetry of that lattice. Table salt is another familiar example: sodium and chloride ions alternate in a repeating cubic lattice, which is why salt crystals tend to form as small cubes.

Crystalline solids are usually grouped into four types based on what holds the lattice together, since this determines their properties. Ionic crystalline solids, like sodium chloride, are held together by ionic bonds between cations and anions, giving them high melting points and brittleness. Molecular crystalline solids, like ice or solid carbon dioxide, are held together by intermolecular forces, dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces, or hydrogen bonding, between discrete molecules, giving them comparatively low melting points. Covalent network crystalline solids, like diamond and quartz, are held together by covalent bonds extending continuously through the entire crystal, giving them extremely high melting points and hardness. Metallic crystalline solids, like copper or iron, are held together by metallic bonding, a lattice of cations surrounded by delocalized electrons, giving them the ability to conduct electricity and to be shaped without shattering.

Because a crystalline solid's particles are locked into one specific, well defined repeating arrangement, all of the attractive forces holding it together need roughly the same amount of thermal energy to break simultaneously. This is why crystalline solids typically melt at a single, sharp temperature rather than softening gradually: quartz melts at approximately 1713 degrees Celsius, and virtually the entire sample transitions from solid to liquid within a very narrow temperature range around that point. This sharp melting behavior is the clearest practical contrast with amorphous solids, which lack this long-range repeating order and, as a result, do not share a single well defined melting point at all.
